questions.q: What did the castle-and-moat model treat as a reliable proxy for trust?
options: The strength of the user's password
Whether the device had endpoint detection and response installed
The number of failed login attempts in the last 24 hours
Network location — being "inside" the perimeter
questions.explain: Perimeter-based security keyed access decisions off network location: if a connection reached the inside of the firewall, it was implicitly trusted.

questions.q: Which assumption did the shift to cloud and SaaS directly break?
options: That resources worth protecting lived physically inside the enterprise's own network boundary
That users should authenticate with a username and password
That firewalls should log denied traffic
That VPNs use encryption
questions.explain: Once CRM, file storage, and line-of-business apps live in SaaS and cloud infrastructure, there's no single owned perimeter left to build a wall around.

questions.q: Why does lateral movement specifically break the castle-and-moat model's security promise, not just its convenience?
options: Because firewalls cannot filter encrypted traffic
Because VPN concentrators are expensive to scale
Because once an attacker is "inside," everything inside the wall was implicitly trusted by design, offering little resistance to moving sideways
Because BYOD devices cannot run antivirus software
questions.explain: The model was never built to stop an adversary who's already past the perimeter — implicit trust inside the boundary is exactly what lets a single compromised credential or device turn into broader access.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does NIST SP 800-207 name as its starting motivation for Zero Trust Architecture?
options: That passwords should be replaced entirely by biometrics
That cloud providers are inherently less secure than on-premises data centers
That multi-factor authentication should be mandatory for all accounts
That the enterprise's resources, users, and devices no longer sit neatly inside one network boundary, so location-based trust can no longer protect what matters
questions.explain: NIST SP 800-207 opens from exactly this premise: de-perimeterization means a model that trusts based on network location can't protect resources that no longer live inside a single boundary.

questions.q: Does this lesson argue that VPNs, NSGs, and firewalls are obsolete under Zero Trust?
options: Yes — Zero Trust architecture removes the need for any network-layer controls
No — those tools remain useful, but network location alone can no longer be the basis for an access decision
Yes, but only for cloud resources, not on-premises ones
No — Zero Trust simply adds a second, redundant perimeter around the first one
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that VPNs, NSGs, and firewalls aren't rejected — what's rejected is treating "reached the network" as equivalent to "should be trusted."
